items.title: A more informative GitHub dashboard
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Since the new dashboard experience became the default, we’ve heard from developers that it used too much space to show too little. Generous padding, wrapped titles, and a low default item count meant extra navigation just to see what needed attention. In addition, “Agent sessions” remained visible even if users didn’t have any agent sessions available. This update makes the dashboard more compact and easier to scan: Pin the Feed or Home tab as your default view. Reduced padding across pull request, issue, and agent session lists so you can see more at a glance. Long titles now stay on one line, with the full text available if you need it. Pull requests and issues now show six items by default instead of three, all while preserving any custom selections you’ve already made. The agent sessions section is hidden if no agent sessions exist on the user’s account. Share your feedback in the Community discussion. The post A more informative GitHub dashboard appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: C++ language server now auto-configures MSBuild builds
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: The Microsoft C++ Language Server for GitHub Copilot CLI now bundles its MSBuild compile commands extractor and invokes it automatically. An agent no longer needs to discover and run a separate configuration skill before it can get precise code intelligence for your project. For more information, including the installation instructions, see the main repository page. What changed Previously, setting up go-to-definition, find references, and other language server features for an MSBuild-based C++ project required you to either provide your own compile_commands.json file or Copilot to locate and run a configuration skill before it could generate a compilation database. That extra discovery step added setup time and consumed tokens before Copilot could start working with your code. Now: The compile commands extractor is bundled directly with the C++ language server, so it’s always available. Copilot invokes the extractor when starting the language server on project open, with no manual or agent-driven setup skill required. Compilation database generation for MSBuild projects is deterministic, reducing setup token usage. Configure other build systems For other build systems, you can provide your own compile_commands.json or use a skill to generate one: For CMake projects, use the generate compile commands skill introduced in the earlier C++ language server release by asking Copilot CLI to “load project.” For custom build systems, follow the guide to create a custom build extractor skill. Get started Follow the Microsoft C++ Language Server quick start to install the plugin and accept the EULA. If your repository contains an MSBuild-based C++ project, Copilot will automatically generate the compilation database it needs for accurate code intelligence. An active GitHub Copilot subscription is required. Help improve the Microsoft C++ Language Server by completing the C++ language server survey. To report a problem or suggest an improvement, open an issue in the Microsoft C+

items.title: Dependabot alerts will pause on inactive repositories
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Starting December 8, 2026, GitHub will turn off Dependabot alerts on most repositories with no activity in the past year. Their existing alerts are archived, not deleted, and you can restore them at any time. With vulnerability discovery and alert volume growing quickly, this keeps Dependabot fast and reliable for the repositories you’re actively developing. What counts as activity GitHub counts any of these as activity: Pushing to any branch or tag Creating the repository Turning on Dependabot alerts Turn alerts back on Any push to the repository automatically turns Dependabot alerts back on. You can also turn them on in the repository’s settings. Either way, GitHub restores the archived alerts, and the one-year clock starts over. Keep alerts on regardless of activity GitHub won’t turn off alerts on repositories with an enforced security configuration that enables Dependabot alerts. It also skips repositories in enterprises whose Dependabot alerts policy doesn’t allow repository administrators to enable or disable alerts. This change applies to all plans on github.com and to GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. For data residency customers, archived alerts are stored in the same region as the rest of your enterprise’s data. It doesn’t apply to GitHub Enterprise Server. The post Dependabot alerts will pause on inactive repositories appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
items.author: Elijah Newren
items.excerpt: Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches. The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git. Vulnerabilities in Git CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name. An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone. The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated. [Advisory] CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally. A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory. Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2. [Advisory] CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures W

items.title: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?
items.author: Gabriele Beltramo
items.excerpt: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space.Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible. It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI, with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5, which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog, this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025, on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.excerpt: Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...] If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2, Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering, anthropic, generative-ai, ai, llms, claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.excerpt: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. items.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: A coding agent opens a pull request and picks an email provider for you. How did it choose? Resend co-founder and CEO Zeno Rocha explores answer engine optimization (AEO) through a concrete example: which email provider does Claude Code recommend, and how does that change across model versions? Then comes the agent experience itself. Once the agent picks Resend, can it find the price, set up the account and send its first email? We also follow an email after the API call succeeds. Zeno explains what happens when Gmail throttles a burst, why a tracking pixel can give you the wrong idea about who opened a message, and how one abusive sender can put other customers’ mail at risk. Then we get into the product decisions: giving an agent 80+ named MCP tools, letting it read pricing in Markdown, and letting it register for a service on its own.
